title: Act III, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Caesar brushes aside the soothsayer ('the ides of March are come') and refuses to read Artemidorus's letter first. Trebonius draws Antony away. Metellus Cimber pleads for his banished brother; Caesar refuses, calling himself 'constant as the northern star.' Casca strikes first; the others stab; Brutus strikes last ('Et tu, Brute? Then fall, Caesar!'). The conspirators bathe their hands in Caesar's blood and cry liberty. Antony sends a servant, then comes himself, shakes their bloody hands and asks to speak at the funeral. Brutus agrees over Cassius's objection, on condition that Antony speaks after him and does not blame them. Alone, Antony prophesies civil war ('Cry Havoc, and let slip the dogs of war'). News comes that Octavius is near Rome.

I must prevent thee, Cimber.
These couchings and these lowly courtesies
Might fire the blood of ordinary men,
And turn pre-ordinance and first decree
Into the law of children. Be not fond,
To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood
That will be thaw’d from the true quality
With that which melteth fools; I mean, sweet words,
Low-crooked court’sies and base spaniel-fawning.
Thy brother by decree is banished:
If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him,
I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.
Know, Caesar doth not wrong, nor without cause
Will he be satisfied.

words.sentence:
Fled to his house amazed:
Men, wives and children stare, cry out and run
As it were doomsday.

Some to the common pulpits, and cry out
“Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!”

Grant that, and then is death a benefit:
So are we Caesar’s friends, that have abridged
His time of fearing death.

segments.script: The real assassination took place on 15 March 44 BC in the Theatre of Pompey, where the Senate was meeting; Shakespeare sets it at the Capitol. The words 'Et tu, Brute?' come from earlier English tradition, not Plutarch. The climax comes at the midpoint of the play. Brutus's second mistake (letting Antony speak) turns the play from a story of conspiracy into one of revenge. Characterization: Caesar compares himself to the "northern star," refusing a petition moments before he is stabbed; "Et tu, Brute? Then fall, Caesar!" Structure: The assassination is the play's centre; afterwards Brutus mistakes Antony's grief for a negotiation and lets him speak at the funeral. Soliloquy: Alone with the body, Antony prophesies "Cry 'Havoc,' and let slip the dogs of war." Watch for warnings ignored: Letters, papers and messages repeatedly warn or move characters, and are repeatedly ignored or misread. In this scene: “He did receive his letters, and is coming; / And bid me say to you by word” (Act III, Scene I, Servant).

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “But I am constant as the northern star” slowly and put it in my own words: Refusing to pardon Metellus's brother, Caesar declares he is as constant as the northern star. Next, craft. I notice the boastful comparison of himself to a fixed star that never moves. The strongest word is “constant”: it means unchanging, which he presents as a godlike virtue. Then, effect. What does Caesar's comparison show moments before his death? My answer: Caesar's comparison of himself to the constant northern star shows his arrogance moments before his death; the line makes his fall look like the punishment of pride.
